This document is candid on purpose.

It is written for two readers: Daniel and Gifty Sogbodjor, the company's co-founders. It names, plainly, the gaps that a 26-year-old company with DS Construction's capability should not still have — and it proposes, concretely, how to close them. Nothing here is for public distribution. The tone is respectful of the legacy first, because the legacy is real and earned; the gaps are named second, because naming them is the only way to fix them.

Positioning DS Construction has built Ghana's institutional buildings for 26 years. The next 26 will not be won by the same engine that won the first.

01 · The Honest Starting Point

What 26 years has — and has not — built.

DS Construction is not a small company that failed. It is a capable company that stopped evolving its structure at some point in the last decade and has been running on founder energy ever since. That distinction matters, because it changes the prescription: this is not a rescue, it is a rebuild of the operating system around a product that already works.

What 26 years has built

Real, durable assets. An in-house fabrication capability that competitors rent. An own vehicle fleet. A blue-chip institutional client list — Ashesi University, University of Ghana, Toyota Ghana, GNAT, Ghana Employers' Association, Glenshire Hills Estate, Asona Enterprises, Government of Ghana projects. A Togo presence. A reputation among licensed architects that has won contracts for over 20 years. These are not small things; most Ghanaian fabricators never acquire them. They are the reason this company deserves a better structure than the one it has.

What 26 years has not built

Almost everything that makes a company outlive its founder. No written strategy beyond a vision statement that still promises to cover all 16 West African countries by 2020. No departmental leadership below the two co-founders. No sales function that is not the co-founders' phones. No succession plan. No corporate headquarters — the company operates from a yard and a postal box. No organised fabrication workshop that a visitor would call world-class. No business development function at all, despite the co-founders' stated ambition to open sites in other parts of Ghana.

The honest reading: DS Construction has been a very good workshop for 26 years. It has never become a company. The transformation proposed here is the work of turning the first into the second — without losing what made the first valuable.

Refined vision · 2031 "By 2031, DS Construction will be Ghana's most trusted institution-grade glazing and facade company — operating from a corporate headquarters and zoned fabrication campuses in at least three Ghanaian regions, led by a named successor, with 40% of revenue from owned channels and 50+ verified client reviews. We will not be the biggest. We will be the one that lasts."

This replaces the expired 2020 vision ("cover all 16 West African countries"). It is a proposal for the founder's approval, not a decision already made.

02 · The Seven Gaps

Named, evidenced, fixable.

Each gap below is stated as the founder and the consultant have observed it, supported where possible by DS's own company profile and the November 2026 marketing audit. Each is followed by what it is costing and what fixing it requires.

Gap 1 — No strategic sales system
Evidence: DS's own company profile lists no sales or business development function; the org chart shows a "Sales and Marketing" box with no named head. The audit scores demand generation 2/10 and reputation 2/10.
  • Revenue is generated by the founder's personal relationships and inbound referrals. There is no pipeline, no stages, no follow-up discipline, no customer list, no spec library for architects.
  • When Daniel is unavailable, sales stop; when Gifty is, operations and finance wait. This is the single biggest revenue risk in the business.
  • Cost: an unknowable but large share of qualified enquiries are lost to slow response, no follow-up, and no documented offer.
Gap 2 — No organisation fit for this era
Evidence: DS's own org chart (company profile, p.4) lists roles — Director/MD, Finance & Administration, Technical Estimator, Workshop Manager, Production & Installation Head, Stores, Procurement, Sales & Marketing, Drivers — but with ~16 listed staff, most of these roles are held by Daniel or Gifty Sogbodjor, or by one person wearing several hats.
  • A 26-year-old company with institutional clients and a Togo operation cannot be run as a two-person partnership with technical staff. The structure that got it here will not carry it forward.
  • There is no HR, no operations manager accountable for the yard, no business development lead, no marketing owner. Everyone reports to the founder.
  • Cost: decisions bottleneck at the founder; the company cannot scale, cannot be audited cleanly, and cannot be handed over.
Gap 3 — No 5- or 10-year goals
Evidence: DS's own website still carries the vision "By 2020 we hope to cover all 16 West African countries" (audit §6.1). The company profile states "over 20 years of excellence" but no forward plan.
  • A stated ambition with a 2020 deadline that has passed and not been replaced is not a strategy — it is a slogan that expired.
  • Without a written 5- and 10-year plan, capital, hiring, facility and succession decisions are made ad hoc, year by year.
  • Cost: the co-founders' stated ambition to open sites in other parts of Ghana has no roadmap, no funding plan, no sequence.
Gap 4 — Fabrication happens in shared space, not a workshop
Evidence: consultant's on-site observation and the co-founders' own description. The Nima yard is enclosed, but its spaces are shared rather than zoned; DS's profile lists "in-house factory" and "own fleet" yet shows no facility photography of an organised plant; the audit notes the brand's strongest real asset is buried.
  • 26 years in, DS still fabricates from one enclosed yard in which material handling, cutting, assembly, finishing and dispatch share the same space — with no flow, no safety zoning, no covered storage and no visitor-ready presentation.
  • A company that sells to architects, institutional buyers and developers cannot invite them to see where their product is made. The factory visit — one of the most powerful sales tools available — is unusable.
  • Cost: lower throughput, higher rework and breakage, safety exposure, and a permanent ceiling on the contract sizes DS can credibly chase.
Gap 5 — No succession plan
Evidence: DS's own company profile names Daniel Sogbodjor (Founder & CEO) and Gifty Sogbodjor (Co-Founder & Deputy MD). No other named leader. Their grown children are not in the business.
  • There is no documented answer to "who runs DS Construction the day the founder steps back?" Not a name, not a plan, not a timeline.
  • Without succession, the company's value is the co-founders' relationships — which means the company has no transferable value. It cannot be sold, financed, or inherited cleanly.
  • Cost: the 26-year legacy is at risk of ending with the founder, regardless of how strong the product is.
Gap 6 — Business development is not a function
Evidence: DS's own company profile and org chart contain no business development role. The audit's growth levers (developer partnerships, architect engagement, referral programme) are all unbuilt.
  • There is no one whose job is to open new accounts, build developer and architect relationships, or take DS into new regions. Growth happens by accident and by the co-founders' personal effort.
  • The co-founders have stated capacity to set up in other parts of Ghana. Capacity without a BD function is just intention.
  • Cost: DS is invisible to the exact buyers (architects, developers, procurement teams) who would specify it for the next 26 years of projects.
Gap 7 — No brand or digital presence worthy of the product
Evidence: audit §6 — website frozen since 2022 (copyright ©2022), zero Google reviews, dormant LinkedIn (5,137 followers, 2–3 years inactive), no Google Business Profile observed, no testimonials.
  • A 26-year company with institutional clients has no verifiable public proof of its own existence. Competitors younger than DS out-present it on every digital surface.
  • Cost: DS loses the "first impression war" on most rival websites and is increasingly excluded from digital-first tender shortlists.
03 · The Cost of Inaction

What happens if nothing changes.

None of the seven gaps is fatal today. Together, and left alone, they are fatal within a generation. The realistic trajectory if DS continues as it is:

Year 1–2Revenue holds on founder relationships and the current client base. No new accounts of significance. The founder works harder for the same or slightly less. Competitors (K3, Emmaldo, Welcraft) continue to win the architect and developer mindshare that DS is not contesting.
Year 3–5The co-founders' energy and health become the binding constraint. Without a sales system, the pipeline empties. The yard, already a bottleneck, cannot take on larger contracts. The first serious competitor overtakes DS in the institutional segment.
Year 5–10Succession is forced by circumstance rather than chosen. The value of the business is the co-founders' relationships, which leave with them. The 26-year legacy is not transferred — it ends.

The audit quantifies the nearer-term leak: indicative GHS 2.6M–14M per year in lost or at-risk revenue across three leaks — visibility, follow-up, and speed/proof — with a mid-case above GHS 5M per year. That is revenue already being earned by competitors or never captured, not hypothetical growth.

The decision is not whether to change. The decision is whether the co-founders choose the timing, the shape and the successor — or whether the market and circumstance choose for them.

Transformation Framework

Five pillars.
One rebuild.

DS Construction Limited · 2026–2031

The transformation is organised into five pillars. Each is independently valuable; together they are the company DS should be by 2031. None requires the co-founders to stop working — all require them to stop being the only people doing the work.

Pillar 1 — Governance & organisation. A structure with named, accountable heads below the founders, and a board that meets.

Pillar 2 — Facility & operations. A corporate HQ and an organised, visitor-ready fabrication workshop.

Pillar 3 — Strategic sales system. A documented, measured, owned sales engine — not the founder's phone.

Pillar 4 — Succession. A named, mentored, prepared successor path with a timeline.

Pillar 5 — Brand & digital. A public presence that matches the product — proof, reviews, spec resources, and a living website.

Five pillars · one rebuild DS Construction · Heritage Portfolio
04 · The Five Pillars

What each pillar requires.

Pillar 1 — Governance & organisation

Adopt a written organisation chart with named heads for: Operations (yard/workshop), Production & Installation, Sales & Business Development, Finance & Administration, and HR/People. Daniel Sogbodjor becomes Managing Director on a board of himself, Gifty Sogbodjor, and two independent advisors — an accountant and an industry peer. Monthly management meetings with a one-page dashboard. Job descriptions and KPIs for every role. This is the single change that makes every other change possible, because it creates owners.

Pillar 2 — Facility & operations

Move from a single enclosed yard to a purpose-built, zoned fabrication campus: covered raw-material storage, cutting and machining bays, assembly and glazing bays, finishing and dispatch, a covered loading area, and a small showroom where architects and buyers can see systems and finishes. Add a corporate office block on the same site — reception, meeting rooms, a spec library, a training room. The co-founders' stated capacity to open other locations in Ghana becomes a real plan only once the Accra plant is a template that can be replicated.

Pillar 3 — Strategic sales system

A documented sales engine: a customer list with history, a qualified-enquiry pipeline with stages, a follow-up discipline, a price list and quotation template, a spec library and technical datasheets for architects, a referral programme, and a review-collection programme. A named Sales & Business Development lead owns it. The consultant's detailed sales system specification (internal document 05) is the implementation reference. Target: 40% of leads from owned channels within 24 months, not referrals alone.

Pillar 4 — Succession

Decide, in writing, who succeeds the founder and on what timeline. Identify the candidate (internal or external), define a 3–5 year mentorship and handover plan, and put the ownership and shareholding question on the table with the family and a lawyer. If the founder's grown children are to be successors, begin their induction into the business now, in defined roles, with real accountability — not as heirs in waiting. If not, plan an external or management buyout. Either is a decision; the absence of a decision is the risk.

Pillar 5 — Brand & digital

A public presence that matches the product: a living website with case studies and spec resources, an active Google Business Profile with reviews, a cleaned-up and active LinkedIn, a WhatsApp-first enquiry channel, and a Heritage Portfolio sent privately to named decision-makers. The audit's 90-day action plan (internal document 03) is the starting sequence. Target: 20+ verified Google reviews and a functioning lead engine within 90 days.

06 · The Facility

Corporate HQ and an organised workshop.

The facility is the visible proof that DS Construction has become a company. It is also, today, the most obvious gap between what DS is and what DS claims to be. The proposal:

Zoned fabrication campus
Organised workshop — visitor-ready
SiteConsolidate on the existing Accra site (13 Onyaa Crescent, Nima) if it can be expanded and reorganised; otherwise acquire a larger plot on the same corridor. Keep the Accra location — it is central to the institutional and corporate client base.
Corporate HQ blockReception, founder's office, meeting rooms, a spec library and sample room, a training room, and open-plan offices for sales, finance and operations. Two storeys. Designed to receive architects and procurement teams.
Fabrication campusZoned, covered bays: raw material storage → cutting/machining → assembly/glazing → finishing → dispatch, with a covered loading bay. Safety zoning, signage, and a visitor walkway so the factory tour becomes a sales tool.
ShowroomA small, curated space showing systems, finishes, glass types and hardware. The place a buyer goes to choose, not just to be told.
ReplicabilityThe Accra plant becomes the template. The co-founders' stated capacity to open sites in other parts of Ghana is realised by replicating this template, not by improvising new yards.
Sequencing note. The facility does not have to be built in one phase. Phase 1 (Year 1): reorganise and cover the existing yard, add safety zoning and a visitor walkway, and build a small showroom and meeting room. Phase 2 (Year 2–3): corporate HQ block. Phase 3 (Year 4–5): second site in another region, using the Accra template.
07 · Succession

Who carries this company next.

Succession is not a document; it is a decision followed by years of preparation. The proposal is a process, not a name — the name is the founder's to choose, and the process is what makes the choice safe.

Step 1 · DecideThe founder states, in writing, whether succession will be family (children), management (an internal leader), or external (a buyer or appointed CEO). This is the founder's decision and no one else's. It should be made within the first 6 months.
Step 2 · PrepareIf family: bring the chosen successor into a real role with real accountability now, with a 3–5 year mentorship plan and a defined handover date. If management: identify the internal candidate and begin the same. If external: begin grooming the business for a clean handover — accounts, contracts, systems, documentation.
Step 3 · FormalisePut ownership, shareholding and the handover timeline into a legal instrument with a lawyer. Include Gifty Sogbodjor in the decision. Include the board.
Step 4 · FundDecide how the successor acquires equity — gift, earn-in, or purchase — and over what period. This is a family conversation that must happen while the founder is in good health and in charge of it.

The risk of not doing this is not that the company fails. The risk is that the founder's life's work becomes an argument among heirs, or is sold for less than it is worth, or simply dissolves. None of those outcomes is necessary.

Companion document

Business Continuity & Key-Person Protection

Succession decides who leads the company next. Continuity decides how the company keeps quoting, fabricating and collecting until that person is ready — or before anyone is. These are separate problems, and this roadmap does not contain the continuity plan.

09 · Sales System

The engine that must exist.

DS Construction's product is strong. Its sales process is the co-founders' phones and memory. The gap between those two is where most of the lost revenue lives. The required system, in priority order:

1. Customer listA single, maintained list of every past and current client with contact, project, value and date. This does not exist today. It is the foundation of everything else.
2. Enquiry pipelineEvery enquiry logged, staged (new → quoted → won/lost), with an owner and a follow-up date. Reviewed weekly by the Sales & BD lead.
3. Quotation templateA standard, branded quotation with scope, systems, warranty and terms. Removes the founder from every quote.
4. Spec libraryTechnical datasheets, system descriptions, glass make-ups and CAD details for architects and QS firms. This is what gets DS specified instead of K3 or Emmaldo.
5. Architect engagementA quarterly factory tour and spec session for architects and specifiers. Low cost, high leverage — specifiers buy on access and trust, not price.
6. Developer partnershipsFormal relationships with 5 estate developers for "windows as standard" supply. A pipeline of repeat work, not one-off jobs.
7. Referral & review programmeAsk every completed job for a Google review at handover; offer a small goodwill gesture for referrals. First mover on reviews in this category wins default trust.

Detailed method, week-by-week, is in the consultant's sales system specification (internal document 05) and the 30-day foundations checklist (client document 03).

11 · SWOT Analysis

Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats.

A SWOT frames the same reality as the gap analysis, from four angles. The strengths and weaknesses are internal and largely within the founder's control; the opportunities and threats are external and must be responded to. Read across the rows: strengths should be used to capture opportunities; weaknesses must be fixed before threats arrive.

Strengths
  • 26 years of continuous operation since 2000 — the oldest credible player in the set.
  • In-house fabrication capability (cuts aluminium up to 3/16") and an own vehicle fleet — assets competitors rent.
  • Blue-chip institutional client list: Ashesi University, University of Ghana, Toyota Ghana, GNAT, Ghana Employers' Association, Glenshire Hills Estate, Asona Enterprises, Government of Ghana projects.
  • Broad product range: windows, doors, curtain walls, uPVC, Alucobond cladding, balustrades, sun breakers, burglar-proof, acoustic ceilings, partitions, frameless shower enclosures.
  • Togo presence and a stated capacity to open sites in other parts of Ghana.
  • Reputation among licensed architects for over 20 years — a channel most competitors never reach.
  • Sole-owned Ghanaian company — a credible nationalistic positioning in a market that values local ownership.
Weaknesses
  • Founder-dependent sales — no pipeline, no stages, no follow-up discipline, no customer list.
  • No departmental leadership below the two founders; ~16 staff, most roles doubled up.
  • No written 5- or 10-year plan; vision statement still promises 16 West African countries by 2020.
  • Fabrication runs from an enclosed but unzoned yard — no corporate HQ, no visitor-ready workshop.
  • No succession plan and no named successor.
  • No business development function at all.
  • Weak digital presence: website frozen since 2022, zero Google reviews, dormant LinkedIn (5,137 followers), no Google Business Profile.
  • No spec library, technical datasheets or CAD details for architects — loses specification to K3 and Emmaldo.
  • Brand under-presented relative to a product that is genuinely strong.
Opportunities
  • Construction GVA forecast +5.2% real growth in 2026; Ghana 7th in SSA by construction GVA.
  • GHS 4.1bn World Bank infrastructure financing and a GHS 4.1bn education/institutional buildout programme — DS's sweet spot.
  • Glazing was a major driver of construction inflation in April 2026 — a talking point for value-led selling (energy efficiency, lifecycle cost).
  • First-mover advantage on Google reviews and Google Maps in Accra — no competitor in the set has a strong review presence.
  • Developer partnerships (the Glenshire model) — formal "windows as standard" supply to estate developers.
  • Togo consolidation and expansion into other Ghana regions, using a replicated Accra template.
  • Architect engagement (quarterly factory tours) — a channel no competitor executes well.
  • AI-enabled, low-cost marketing (WhatsApp funnels, AI content) — affordable for a company this size.
  • Energy-efficient / double-glazing story as Ghana's heat and noise problem worsens.
Threats
  • Near-term demand softness: Q1 2026 construction growth only 1.3%; cement sales down 10.3% Jan–Jul 2026.
  • Active challengers (K3 Aluproducts, Emmaldo, Welcraft, AluMaster, Alubond) winning the digital shelf and tender shortlists.
  • Tender and specifier shortlists are increasingly digital-first — DS is invisible where buyers look.
  • Material and cost inflation squeezing margins; cedi volatility and import duties on aluminium profiles.
  • Informal, price-cutting fabricators competing on price for residential work.
  • Key-person risk: the company's value is the co-founders' relationships, which are not transferable.
  • Referral dependence in a softening market — fewer projects to go around.

Strategic implications

Use the strengths to capture the opportunities. DS's institutional credibility and in-house capability are exactly what the education and infrastructure buildout (GHS 4.1bn) requires. The fix is visibility and access, not product.

Fix the weaknesses before the threats arrive. The threats are already here — soft demand and digital-first competitors. The weaknesses (no sales system, no digital presence, no successor) are the reason DS cannot respond. The 5-year roadmap exists to close that gap in time.

The decisive variable is the founding pair. Every strength traces to what Daniel and Gifty Sogbodjor built; every weakness traces to the company having never grown beyond them. The transformation is therefore not a marketing project — it is a leadership transition, and they are the only people who can authorise it.

— · Closing

The decision in front of the co-founders.

DS Construction has earned the right to a better structure. Twenty-six years of institutional work, an in-house factory, an own fleet, a blue-chip client list and a reputation among licensed architects — these are not the assets of a small company. They are the assets of a company that has never been organised as one.

The transformation proposed here is not a rebrand and not a marketing exercise. It is the work of turning a founder-led workshop into a future-ready company: governance, facility, sales system, succession, and brand. Each pillar is independently valuable. Together they are what makes DS Construction worth more in 2031 than it is today — and worth something at all the day the founder decides to step back.

The decision is theirs, and only theirs. The consultant's role is to make the gaps visible, to propose the structure, and to walk alongside if invited. The legacy is already built. The only question is whether it will be carried forward.

"The proof is already built.
Our only job is to make the company worthy of it."
